procedural_history.impugned_order: Order of reversion and subsequent dismissal from service
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The Trial Court dismissed the suit. The High Court on appeal reversed the decision of the trial court on the finding that the reversion was not in the usual course or for administrative reasons but it was after the finding on an inquiry about some complaint against the plaintiff and by way of punishment to him. The order of dismissal was set aside on the ground that it had been made by the Deputy Inspector General while the appointing authority in the case of the post of Subedar-Major was the Inspector General so that there was a violation of Art. 311 (I).
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellants (likely the Deputy Inspector General or the government) appealed the High Court's decision to the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, upholding the High Court's decision that the reversion was void and the subsequent dismissal violated Art. 311(1) of the Constitution.

directions: The appeal is dismissed with costs.

issue.issue_text: Whether the test to determine if a reversion order is punitive is to see if the alleged misconduct was the mere motive for the order or its very foundation.

facts: An employee was reverted from an officiating post to his substantive post. The reversion order itself did not contain any express words of stigma or mention any misconduct.
However, the reversion followed a report concerning an alleged assault by the employee on his orderly.
The employee argued that this reversion was a punishment, while the employer argued it was a routine administrative decision, and the form of the order should be considered conclusive.
law: The Supreme Court rejected the argument that the form of a reversion order is conclusive in determining whether it is punitive.
The Court stated that an order which is "innocuous on the face" and does not contain any imputation of misconduct might merely be a "cloak or camouflage for an order founded on misconduct."
To determine the true nature of the order, the "entirety of circumstances preceding or attendant on the impugned order must be examined."
The Court affirmed that the "overriding test" is to determine whether the alleged misconduct was a "mere motive" for the order of reversion or its "very foundation."
application: Applying this test, the Court examined the circumstances leading to the reversion.
It found that the order of reversion was "directly and proximately founded on" the reports concerning the employee's conduct, particularly the incident of assault.
Therefore, the misconduct was not just a background motive but the very foundation of the decision to revert the employee.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court accepted and applied the test, holding that to determine if a reversion order is punitive, a court must look beyond the form of the order to the surrounding circumstances. The overriding test is whether the employee's misconduct was the mere motive for the order or its very foundation. Since the employee's misconduct was the foundation for the reversion in this case, the order was deemed punitive.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the test to determine if a reversion order is punitive is to see if the alleged misconduct was the mere motive for the order or its very foundation.
appellant_arguments: The order of reversion is not punitive because it casts no aspersion on the respondent's character or integrity on its face.
Even if the motive for the reversion was the report of misconduct (the assault on the orderly), it does not make the order punitive.
The court should only look at the form of the order, and if it does not contain any imputation of misconduct or words of stigma, it must be held to be a routine administrative action.
The fact that no formal departmental enquiry was held before the reversion supports the argument that it was not a punishment.
respondent_arguments: The form of the order is not conclusive of its true nature and can be a 'cloak or camouflage' for an order founded on misconduct.
The court must examine the entirety of the circumstances preceding and attendant to the order to discover its real purpose.
The overriding test is whether the misconduct was a mere motive for the order or its very foundation.

cases.case_name: State of Punjab & Anr. v. Shri Suraj Raj Bahadur
cases.principle: The overriding test to determine if an order is punitive is whether the misconduct is a mere motive or is the very foundation of the order.

cases.case_name: S. R. Tewari v. District Board Agra & Anr.
cases.principle: The form of an order is not conclusive of its true nature and it might merely be a cloak or camouflage for an order founded on misconduct.

cases.case_name: Champaklal Chimanlal Shah v. The Union of India
cases.principle: To determine if an order is punitive, one must examine whether misconduct was a mere motive for the termination of service or the very foundation of the order.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The form of an order is not conclusive of its true nature, as it might be a cloak or camouflage for an order founded on misconduct. The entirety of the circumstances preceding or attendant on an impugned order must be examined, and the overriding test is whether the misconduct is a mere motive for the order or is the very foundation of the order.
obiter: An order which is innocuous on its face and does not contain any imputation of misconduct is a circumstance or a piece of evidence for finding whether it was made by way of punishment or administrative routine.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court's determination of whether a reversion order is punitive does not depend solely on the form of the order. An order that appears innocuous on its face may merely be a 'cloak or camouflage' for an action founded on misconduct. Therefore, a court must examine the entirety of the circumstances preceding and attendant to the order to discover its true nature and determine if the alleged misconduct was the mere motive for the order or its very foundation.
legal_tests_applied: The overriding test will always be whether the misconduct is a mere motive or is the very foundation of the order.
why_appellant_lost: The court rejected the rigid principle that one has only to look to the order and if it does not contain any imputation of misconduct or words of stigma, it must be held to be a routine administrative action.

The court found that the precedent the appellant relied on (Dhaba's case) is not an authority for the proposition that so long as there are no express words of stigma in the order, it cannot be held to have been made by way of punishment.
The court is not debarred from looking at all the attendant circumstances to discover whether the order had been made by way of punishment.
why_respondent_won: The court accepted that the form of the order is not conclusive of its true nature and it might merely be a cloak or camouflage for an order founded on misconduct.
The court affirmed that the entirety of circumstances preceding or attendant on the impugned order must be examined to determine its real purpose.
Applying the 'motive vs. foundation' test, the court agreed with the High Court that the order of reversion was directly and proximately founded on the reports concerning the respondent's misconduct.
policy_considerations: Courts must look beyond the mere form of an administrative order to its substance to prevent the government from circumventing constitutional protections for its employees by using carefully worded orders to disguise punitive actions as routine administrative matters.
